title: 📐 Geometry Design Studio
description: Welcome to the Geometry Design Studio! You have been hired as a junior architect at a creative design firm. Every project — from park layouts to building facades — requires you to master shapes, angles, area, perimeter, symmetry, and coordinates. Sketch it right, and your designs will win the big showcase!
subject: mathematics
how_to_play: You are a junior architect working on 14 design projects — every one involves geometry!
Each round presents a design challenge where you must use shapes, angles, and measurements to make decisions.
Watch your dashboard — your Design Stations, Tools, and Client Satisfaction are interconnected.
NPCs like Architect Ananya (mentor), Builder Raj, Picky Client Priya, and Intern Dev react to your choices.
Random events like design competitions and surprise client visits will test your geometry skills.
Keep your Geometry Accuracy high — wrong measurements mean failed designs and lost contracts!
learning_objectives: Identify and classify 2D shapes including triangles, quadrilaterals, and circles
Calculate the perimeter of regular and irregular polygons
Calculate the area of rectangles, triangles, and composite shapes
Measure and classify angles as acute, right, obtuse, or straight
Identify lines of symmetry and create symmetrical designs
Plot and read coordinates on a grid to position design elements
cultural_context: Architecture and design studio setting connecting geometry to real-world Indian urban planning, rangoli patterns, and city design

behaviors.message: Your geometry fundamentals need work! Remember, every shape has properties — sides, angles, and measurements. A rectangle has 4 right angles and opposite sides are equal. Let me demonstrate with a model.
Too many measurement errors in your designs! If a client asks for a room that is 6 metres by 4 metres, the area must be exactly 24 square metres — not 'roughly 24.' Measure twice, draw once!
Excellent progress! Your understanding of shapes and measurements is really growing. I can see your angles are precise and your area calculations are spot on. Keep this up!
You are a geometry prodigy! Your designs are mathematically flawless — perfect symmetry, accurate areas, precise angles. I might make you lead architect on the next big project!
I cannot build from these plans! The perimeter measurements do not add up — you wrote 20 metres but the sides only total 18. If the blueprint is wrong, the building will be wrong!
Now these are blueprints I can work with! Every angle is marked, every measurement is correct. The construction crew loves when the geometry is right — it saves time and money!
Every contractor in the city wants to work with your studio! Your blueprints are the gold standard — precise geometry means zero rework. You have made my job a pleasure!
I specifically asked for a rectangular garden with area 48 square metres, and your design shows 42! Do you not know how to multiply length times width? I want this redesigned immediately!

Now THIS is what I envisioned! The symmetry in the facade is perfect, the angles are crisp, and you even added a creative tessellation pattern to the floor. I am telling all my friends about your studio!

I have recommended your studio to the city planning committee! Your geometric precision is unmatched. The tessellation you designed for my lobby floor is a work of art. You understand that geometry IS art!
I cannot figure out the difference between a rhombus and a rectangle. They both have four sides! Can you help me understand what makes each quadrilateral special?
Everyone is so stressed. I accidentally drew a right angle as 80 degrees and the whole team was upset. I know I need more practice with the protractor, but I am trying...
I finally get it! A square IS a rectangle — it is a special rectangle where all four sides are equal. And a rhombus IS a parallelogram with all equal sides! You are the best teacher!

I just calculated the area of a composite shape all by myself! I split it into a rectangle and a triangle, found each area, and added them together. Thank you for teaching me — I want to be an architect someday!

rounds.situation: It is your first day at the Geometry Design Studio! Architect Ananya welcomes you and gives you a tour. Your very first task: a client wants a rectangular name board for their shop. 'I need it exactly 80 cm long and 30 cm wide,' they say. Sounds simple — but do you know what a rectangle really is, and what makes it different from other shapes?
rounds.goal: Learn the basic properties of 2D shapes by designing your first rectangular sign.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: A 2D shape is flat — it has length and width but no thickness. A rectangle has 4 sides, 4 right angles (90 degrees each), and opposite sides that are equal. Knowing shape properties is the foundation of all geometry.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What makes a rectangle different from a square? What do they have in common?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon architecture studio on the first day, young designer at a drafting table with ruler and pencil, Architect Ananya pointing at a blueprint, colorful geometric posters on walls, Pixar-style, welcoming atmosphere

choices.label: A. A rectangle has 4 sides, 4 right angles (90°), and opposite sides are equal and parallel
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A rectangle has 4 sides with 4 right angles (each 90°). Opposite sides are equal in length AND parallel. A square is a special rectangle where ALL 4 sides are equal. These properties make rectangles perfect for buildings and rooms!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. A rectangle has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 That describes a SQUARE, not a rectangle! A rectangle has 4 right angles, but only OPPOSITE sides are equal (length = length, width = width). A square has ALL 4 sides equal and is actually a special type of rectangle.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. A rectangle has 4 sides and its angles can be any size
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 That describes a general quadrilateral (4-sided shape), not specifically a rectangle. What makes a rectangle special is that ALL 4 angles must be RIGHT ANGLES (90°). Also, opposite sides must be equal and parallel.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: D. A rectangle has 2 pairs of parallel sides but no right angles
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A shape with 2 pairs of parallel sides but no right angles is a PARALLELOGRAM (like a slanted rectangle). A rectangle MUST have right angles (90°). In fact, a rectangle IS a parallelogram — just one with all 90° angles.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

rounds.situation: Architect Ananya gives you a challenge: create a 'Shape Catalogue' poster for the studio wall. It must show examples of every 2D shape the studio uses — triangles, rectangles, squares, circles, pentagons, and hexagons. Each shape must be labelled with its name and number of sides.
rounds.goal: Identify and classify all major 2D shapes by their properties.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: 2D shapes are everywhere in architecture. Triangles have 3 sides, quadrilaterals have 4, pentagons have 5, hexagons have 6. Circles have no straight sides at all! Learning to recognize and name shapes is the first step to using them.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Look around the room you are in right now. How many different 2D shapes can you spot? Which shape appears most often?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon wall poster showing colorful labeled 2D shapes — triangle, rectangle, square, circle, pentagon, hexagon — young designer arranging them neatly, bright studio, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. 135° is an obtuse angle (between 90° and 180°)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Angle types: Acute = less than 90° (sharp). Right = exactly 90° (L-shape). Obtuse = between 90° and 180° (wide). Straight = exactly 180° (flat line). Reflex = between 180° and 360° (more than half turn). 135° is between 90° and 180°, so it's obtuse!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. 135° is an acute angle because it's a sharp angle
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Acute angles are LESS than 90° (think 'a cute little angle'). 135° is much bigger than 90°, so it's OBTUSE. Obtuse angles are between 90° and 180° — they look wide and open. Example: 45° is acute, 135° is obtuse.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. 135° is a reflex angle because it's bigger than 90°
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A reflex angle is bigger than 180° (more than a straight line), not just bigger than 90°. 135° is between 90° and 180°, making it OBTUSE. Reflex angles are 180°-360°, like 270° (three-quarter turn).

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: D. 135° is a straight angle because it's close to 180°
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A straight angle is EXACTLY 180° — it looks like a flat line. 135° is not 180°. Being 'close to' a value doesn't count in geometry! 135° is an OBTUSE angle (between 90° and 180°). Remember: straight = precisely 180°.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

rounds.situation: A client wants a house with a triangular roof. But there are many types of triangles! An equilateral triangle has all sides equal. An isosceles triangle has two equal sides. A scalene triangle has no equal sides. The client asks: 'Which triangle shape would make the strongest, most beautiful roof?'
rounds.goal: Understand the different types of triangles and their properties.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Triangles are classified by their sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by their angles (acute, right, obtuse). An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides and 3 equal angles of 60 degrees each. Choosing the right triangle depends on the purpose.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do you think triangles are used so often in construction and bridges? What makes them strong?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon house designs showing three different triangular roof shapes — equilateral, isosceles, and scalene — young architect comparing them with measuring tape, colorful houses, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. The angle measures 65° — I used the inner scale starting from 0° on the baseline
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ To use a protractor: (1) Place the center point on the vertex of the angle. (2) Align the baseline with one arm of the angle. (3) Read from 0° — if the angle is acute (less than 90°), use the scale that starts at 0° on your baseline side. 65° is an acute angle. ✓

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. The angle measures 115° — I read the outer scale instead
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Protractors have two scales (inner and outer) that go in opposite directions. If the angle looks acute (less than 90°), your reading should be less than 90°. Reading 115° for an acute angle means you used the wrong scale! 65° + 115° = 180° — the scales always add up to 180°.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. The angle measures 55° — I started counting from 10° by mistake
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Always make sure your baseline arm starts at exactly 0° on the protractor. If you start counting from 10°, your reading will be 10° less than the actual angle. The correct reading is 65°. Double-check that the 0° mark lines up with your baseline!

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. The angle is about 65 cm — protractors measure in centimeters
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Protractors measure ANGLES in DEGREES (°), not lengths in centimeters! A ruler measures length (cm, mm). A protractor measures how wide an angle opens, in degrees. The answer is 65° (65 degrees). Angles are measured by rotation, not distance.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

rounds.situation: A school is being renovated and they want unique window shapes for each floor. The principal says: 'Ground floor gets square windows. First floor gets rectangular windows. Second floor gets parallelogram windows. Top floor gets trapezoid windows.' You need to design all four quadrilateral window types!
rounds.goal: Understand different types of quadrilaterals — squares, rectangles, parallelograms, and trapezoids.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: All quadrilaterals have 4 sides, but their properties differ. A square has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles. A rectangle has opposite sides equal and 4 right angles. A parallelogram has opposite sides equal and parallel. A trapezoid has exactly one pair of parallel sides.
rounds.reflection_prompt: A square is a special type of rectangle. Can you explain why? Is every rectangle also a square?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon school building with four floors, each floor having different shaped windows — squares, rectangles, parallelograms, trapezoids — young architect pointing at blueprint, colorful building, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. Perimeter = 12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40 cm (add all 4 sides of the rectangle)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Perimeter is the total distance AROUND a shape — add up all the sides. Rectangle with length 12 cm and width 8 cm: P = 12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40 cm. Shortcut formula: P = 2 × (length + width) = 2 × (12 + 8) = 2 × 20 = 40 cm.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. Perimeter = 12 × 8 = 96 cm (multiply length times width)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Length × width gives you the AREA (space inside), not the perimeter (distance around). Perimeter = add all sides. For a rectangle: P = 2(l + w) = 2(12 + 8) = 40 cm. Area would be 12 × 8 = 96 cm².

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. Perimeter = 12 + 8 = 20 cm (add length and width)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You only added 2 sides, but a rectangle has 4 sides! Opposite sides are equal, so there are TWO lengths (12) and TWO widths (8). P = 12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40 cm, or P = 2 × (12 + 8) = 40 cm. Don't forget the other two sides!

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. Perimeter = 4 × 12 = 48 cm (multiply one side by 4)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Multiplying one side by 4 only works for a SQUARE (where all sides are equal). A rectangle has TWO different side lengths. P = 2 × (length + width) = 2 × (12 + 8) = 2 × 20 = 40 cm, not 48 cm.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

widget_answer.prompt: Calculate the area of the rectangle (6cm x 4cm)

rounds.situation: The city building inspector visits the studio. He needs to verify that ALL angles in your recent designs are correct. 'Show me you understand angles,' he says. 'What is a right angle? An acute angle? An obtuse angle? A straight angle?' If you cannot answer, the studio could lose its license!
rounds.goal: Identify and classify angles: acute (less than 90°), right (exactly 90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°), and straight (exactly 180°).
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Angles are measured in degrees. A right angle is exactly 90° — like the corner of a book. Acute means less than 90° (think 'a cute little angle'). Obtuse means more than 90° but less than 180°. A straight angle is exactly 180° — a flat line.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Can a triangle have two obtuse angles? Why or why not?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon building inspector with protractor checking angles on a blueprint, young architect demonstrating angle types on a whiteboard — acute, right, obtuse, straight — official inspection scene, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. Area = 15 × 9 = 135 cm² (length × width)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The area of a rectangle = length × width. For a room that is 15 cm long and 9 cm wide: Area = 15 × 9 = 135 cm². Area measures the space INSIDE the shape and is always in square units (cm²). Think of it as counting 1cm × 1cm squares that fit inside!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Area = 2 × (15 + 9) = 48 cm (the formula is 2 × length + width)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 That's the PERIMETER formula, not area! Perimeter = 2(l + w) = distance around. Area = l × w = space inside. For this rectangle: Perimeter = 2(15+9) = 48 cm, but Area = 15 × 9 = 135 cm². Also, area uses cm² (square units), not cm.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. Area = 15 + 9 = 24 cm² (add the two sides)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Area requires MULTIPLICATION, not addition. Adding the sides just gives you part of the perimeter. Area = length × width = 15 × 9 = 135 cm². Think of it this way: 15 rows of 9 squares each = 135 little squares inside.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: D. Area = 15 × 9 = 135 cm (length × width)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The calculation 15 × 9 = 135 is right, but the unit is wrong! Area must be in SQUARE units: cm², not cm. When you multiply cm × cm, you get cm² (square centimeters). Perimeter is in cm, but area is always in cm². The correct answer is 135 cm².

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

challenge.question: What is the area of a rectangle with length 8 cm and width 5 cm?

rounds.situation: The city council hires your studio to design a new park! First task: calculate how much fencing is needed to go around the entire park boundary. The park is an L-shape — a big rectangle (60m × 40m) with a smaller rectangle (20m × 20m) cut out of one corner. What is the total perimeter?
rounds.goal: Calculate the perimeter of regular and composite (L-shaped) polygons.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Perimeter means the total distance around the outside of a shape. For a rectangle, perimeter = 2 × (length + width). For composite shapes, you must carefully trace the outside boundary and add up every side length. Drawing it out helps!
rounds.reflection_prompt: If two shapes have the same area, do they always have the same perimeter? Can you think of an example?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon aerial view of an L-shaped park with fencing being measured around the boundary, young architect with measuring tape, numbers labeling each side, colorful park with trees and playground, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. Area = ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm² (half of base times height)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height. With base = 10 cm and height = 6 cm: Area = ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm². Why ½? Because a triangle is exactly half of a rectangle with the same base and height (10 × 6 = 60, half = 30).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. Area = 10 × 6 = 60 cm² (just multiply base times height)
choices.learning_concept: Triangle Area — Don't Forget the Half
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 That would be the area of a RECTANGLE (base × height = 60 cm²). A triangle is only HALF of that rectangle. So: Area = ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm². The ½ is crucial — imagine cutting a rectangle diagonally; each triangle is half the rectangle.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. Area = 10 + 6 + 8 = 24 cm (add all three sides of the triangle)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Adding all three sides gives you the PERIMETER (distance around), not the area. Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height = ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm². Note: the height is the PERPENDICULAR distance from the base to the opposite point, not a side length.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: D. Area = ½ × (10 + 6) = 8 cm² (half of the sum of base and height)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The formula is ½ × base × height (multiply!), not ½ × (base + height). The correct calculation: ½ × 10 × 6 = ½ × 60 = 30 cm². Multiplying base × height gives the rectangle area; halving it gives the triangle area.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! The city council moved the park project deadline up by a week! You now have just ONE DAY to finish the full park layout — calculating areas for the playground zone, garden zone, and walking path zone. Builder Raj is panicking because he needs final measurements TODAY. Ananya is on the phone with the council. Dev looks terrified. Every measurement must be right — there is no time for errors!
rounds.goal: Apply all your geometry skills under extreme time pressure — perimeter, area, and shape identification simultaneously!
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Real-world geometry happens under pressure. When you truly understand shapes, angles, and measurements — not just memorize formulas — you can perform even when stressed. Deep understanding beats surface memorization.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does truly understanding geometry (not just memorizing formulas) help you work faster under pressure?
rounds.image_prompt: Chaotic cartoon architecture studio with deadline countdown clock on wall, blueprints scattered everywhere, multiple designers working frantically, stressed but determined young architect at drafting table, Pixar-style dramatic scene

choices.label: A. Area ≈ 3.14 × 7 × 7 = 153.86 cm² (using πr² with r = 7)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Area of a circle = π × r² (pi times radius squared). With radius = 7 cm: Area = 3.14 × 7² = 3.14 × 49 = 153.86 cm². Remember: r² means r × r (7 × 7 = 49), and π ≈ 3.14. The radius is half the diameter!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.delayed_gratification: Prioritizing long-term gains over short-term comfort builds character.

choices.label: B. Area = 3.14 × 14 × 14 = 615.44 cm² (using the diameter instead of radius)
choices.learning_concept: Radius vs Diameter in Circle Area
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You used the diameter (14) instead of the radius (7)! The formula is πr², where r = RADIUS (half the diameter). Radius = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm. So: Area = 3.14 × 7² = 3.14 × 49 = 153.86 cm². Using the diameter gives you 4× the correct area!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. Area = 3.14 × 7 = 21.98 cm² (just multiply π times radius)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You forgot to SQUARE the radius! The formula is π × r², not π × r. r² means r × r. So: 7² = 7 × 7 = 49. Then: 3.14 × 49 = 153.86 cm². Note: π × r (without squaring) would give you half the circumference, not the area.

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: D. Area = 2 × 3.14 × 7 = 43.96 cm (that's the circle formula)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 2πr is the CIRCUMFERENCE formula (distance around the circle), not the area. Circumference = 2 × 3.14 × 7 = 43.96 cm. But AREA = πr² = 3.14 × 7² = 3.14 × 49 = 153.86 cm². Different formulas for different measurements!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

widget_answer.prompt: Calculate the area of the circle (radius 3cm, use pi=3.14159)

rounds.situation: The school principal is back! She wants to tile the floors of three classrooms with square tiles. Classroom A is 8m × 6m. Classroom B is 10m × 5m. Classroom C is 7m × 7m. Each tile covers 1 square metre. How many tiles does each classroom need? And which classroom has the largest area?
rounds.goal: Calculate the area of rectangles and squares using length × width.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Area measures how much surface a shape covers. For rectangles: Area = length × width. For squares: Area = side × side. Area is measured in square units (sq m, sq cm). 8m × 6m = 48 square metres — that is how many 1m × 1m tiles you need.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Classroom B (10m × 5m) and Classroom A (8m × 6m) — which has more area? Which has more perimeter? Can a smaller perimeter hold a bigger area?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon classroom being tiled, grid of colorful square tiles on floor, young architect counting tiles with calculator, measurements labeled on walls (8m × 6m), bright school setting, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. A square has 4 lines of symmetry — vertical, horizontal, and 2 diagonals
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A square has 4 lines of symmetry: 1 vertical (top to bottom), 1 horizontal (left to right), and 2 diagonal (corner to corner). A line of symmetry divides a shape into two mirror-image halves. If you fold along any of these lines, both halves match perfectly!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.creativity: Not settling for the obvious solution builds creative problem-solving.

choices.label: B. A square has 2 lines of symmetry — just vertical and horizontal
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You found 2 lines but missed the other 2! A square also has symmetry along its diagonals (corner to corner). That's 4 total: vertical, horizontal, and 2 diagonals. Compare: a rectangle has only 2 lines of symmetry (vertical + horizontal, but NOT the diagonals).

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. A square has 8 lines of symmetry — through every corner and side
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 A square has exactly 4 lines of symmetry, not 8. The 4 lines are: vertical center, horizontal center, and 2 diagonals. A regular octagon (8 sides) has 8 lines of symmetry. In general, a regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry.

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. A square has 1 line of symmetry — only down the middle vertically
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 The vertical line IS a line of symmetry, but it's not the only one! Try folding a square horizontally — it matches. Try folding along a diagonal — it also matches! A square has 4 lines of symmetry: vertical, horizontal, and 2 diagonals.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

rounds.situation: Client Priya wants a triangular garden in her backyard. She says: 'The base should be 12 metres and the height should be 8 metres. How much grass do I need to cover it?' This is an area problem — but triangles use a different formula than rectangles! Can you figure out the area of a triangle?
rounds.goal: Calculate the area of triangles using the formula: Area = 1/2 × base × height.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: A triangle is exactly HALF of a rectangle with the same base and height. That is why the area formula is 1/2 × base × height. For Priya's garden: 1/2 × 12 × 8 = 48 square metres. The '1/2' is the key — always remember to halve it!
rounds.reflection_prompt: If a rectangle and a triangle have the same base and same height, the triangle always has exactly half the area. Why?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon triangular garden in a backyard, grass being laid in a triangle shape, measurements shown (base 12m, height 8m), Client Priya watching, young architect with measuring tape, colorful backyard, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. A cuboid has 6 faces, 12 edges, and 8 vertices (corners)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A cuboid (box shape) has: 6 faces (flat surfaces — top, bottom, front, back, left, right), 12 edges (lines where faces meet), and 8 vertices (corners). Euler's formula checks this: Faces + Vertices - Edges = 6 + 8 - 12 = 2 ✓. A cube is a special cuboid with all square faces.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. A cuboid has 4 faces, 8 edges, and 4 vertices
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 That sounds more like a 2D rectangle! A cuboid is a 3D box. It has 6 faces (not 4) — don't forget the top and bottom! It has 12 edges (4 along the length, 4 along the width, 4 vertical) and 8 vertices (4 on top + 4 on bottom).

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. A cuboid has 6 faces, 8 edges, and 12 vertices
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You swapped edges and vertices! A cuboid has 12 EDGES (lines) and 8 VERTICES (corners), not the other way around. Vertices are the corner points (8 of them), and edges are the lines connecting them (12 of them). Remember: V=8, E=12, F=6.

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. A cuboid has 6 faces, 6 edges, and 6 vertices
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Only the faces are 6! A cuboid has 12 edges and 8 vertices. Trick to remember: hold a box. Count corners (vertices) = 8 (4 on top + 4 on bottom). Count edge lines = 12 (4 top edges + 4 bottom edges + 4 vertical edges).

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

challenge.question: A triangle has a base of 12 cm and height of 6 cm. What is its area?

rounds.situation: Your studio is designing a grand entrance gate for a community hall. The gate MUST be perfectly symmetrical — the left side must be a mirror image of the right side. Ananya explains: 'Symmetry means if you draw a line down the middle, both halves are identical. Find the line of symmetry!' But your first draft is lopsided. Can you fix it?
rounds.goal: Understand lines of symmetry and create symmetrical designs.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: A line of symmetry divides a shape into two identical halves that are mirror images of each other. A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry, a square has 4, and a circle has infinite! An equilateral triangle has 3 lines of symmetry. Symmetry creates balance and beauty.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Which letters of the English alphabet have a vertical line of symmetry? Which have a horizontal line of symmetry? Which have both?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon grand entrance gate design split down the middle with a dotted symmetry line, left side matching right side perfectly, young architect using a mirror to check symmetry, colorful community hall, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. Volume = 8 × 5 × 3 = 120 cm³ (length × width × height)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height. For a box 8 cm × 5 cm × 3 cm: Volume = 8 × 5 × 3 = 120 cm³. Volume measures 3D space inside and uses CUBIC units (cm³). Think of it as stacking layers: 8×5 = 40 cubes per layer × 3 layers = 120 tiny cubes.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Volume = 2(8+5+3) = 32 cm (add all dimensions and double)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Adding dimensions is related to perimeter/edges, not volume. Volume = l × w × h = 8 × 5 × 3 = 120 cm³. Volume needs MULTIPLICATION of all three dimensions because we're filling 3D space. The unit is cm³ (cubic centimeters).

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: C. Volume = 8 × 5 = 40 cm² (just multiply length and width)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 8 × 5 = 40 cm² gives you the AREA of the base (floor), not the volume. Volume needs all THREE dimensions: l × w × h = 8 × 5 × 3 = 120 cm³. Think: area is flat (2D, cm²), volume fills space (3D, cm³).

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: D. Volume = 8 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm³ (add all three numbers)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Volume uses multiplication, not addition. Adding gives only 16, but the correct volume is 8 × 5 × 3 = 120 cm³. Imagine filling the box with 1cm cubes: you'd fit 8 across, 5 deep, and 3 high = 120 cubes total.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

widget_answer.prompt: Calculate the area of the triangle (base 6cm, height 5cm)

rounds.situation: The city council wants you to create a digital map of the new neighbourhood! Everything must be placed on a coordinate grid. The school goes at position (3, 7). The hospital at (8, 2). The park at (1, 5). The fire station at (6, 9). Can you read and plot coordinates correctly to create the perfect city map?
rounds.goal: Plot and read coordinates on a grid — understanding that (x, y) means 'go right x, then go up y'.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Coordinates use an ordered pair (x, y). The first number (x) tells you how far to go across (horizontal). The second number (y) tells you how far to go up (vertical). Always go across first, then up — think 'along the corridor, then up the stairs.'
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the difference between the point (3, 5) and the point (5, 3)? Why does the order of numbers matter?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon city map on a coordinate grid, colorful buildings placed at marked coordinates, young architect plotting a point with pencil, grid lines visible with numbered axes, Pixar-style, bright cityscape

choices.label: A. Point (4, 7) means go 4 units right on the x-axis, then 7 units up on the y-axis
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ In coordinates (x, y), the first number (x) tells you how far to go RIGHT, and the second number (y) tells you how far to go UP. For (4, 7): start at the origin (0,0), go 4 right along the x-axis, then 7 up parallel to the y-axis. Memory tip: x comes before y, just like in the alphabet!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. Point (4, 7) means go 7 units right, then 4 units up
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You swapped x and y! In (4, 7), the FIRST number (4) is x (horizontal/right) and the SECOND number (7) is y (vertical/up). Remember: 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' — x first (along), then y (up).

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: C. Point (4, 7) means the point is at 4+7 = 11 units from the origin
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Coordinates give you DIRECTIONS (right and up), not a total distance. (4, 7) means go 4 right AND 7 up — these are two separate movements. Adding them together loses the directional information. You need BOTH numbers to find the exact position.

skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: D. Point (4, 7) means go 4 units left, then 7 units down
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Positive numbers go RIGHT (x) and UP (y). Left would be negative x, and down would be negative y. So (4, 7) = 4 right + 7 up. (-4, -7) would be 4 left + 7 down. The signs tell you the direction!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! Client Priya calls in a panic — the floor tiles for her new office were ordered based on YOUR area calculations, but nothing fits! She says the room is 9m × 7m and you calculated 56 square metres, but the tiles do not cover the floor. You check your work and realize you wrote 8 × 7 = 56 instead of 9 × 7 = 63! A 7 square metre error that cost real money! How do you fix this?
rounds.goal: Understand the real-world consequences of geometry errors and learn to double-check calculations.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Everyone makes mistakes in mathematics. What matters is how you respond. A professional checks their work, admits errors honestly, and fixes them. One small number error (writing 8 instead of 9) caused a 7 sq m gap. Always double-check critical measurements!
rounds.reflection_prompt: What checking methods could prevent calculation errors? Why is it important to admit mistakes honestly?
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon office floor with tiles that do not quite cover the whole area, gap visible in corner, worried young architect on phone with Client Priya, calculator and blueprints on floor, dramatic scene, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. Parallel lines never meet and are always the same distance apart; perpendicular lines meet at 90°
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Parallel lines go in the same direction and NEVER intersect — like railway tracks (symbol: ∥). Perpendicular lines cross at exactly 90° (a right angle) — like the corner of a book (symbol: ⊥). In a rectangle, opposite sides are parallel AND adjacent sides are perpendicular!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Parallel lines cross at 90° and perpendicular lines never meet
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 You swapped the definitions! PARALLEL = never meet (think: train tracks running side by side). PERPENDICULAR = meet at 90° (think: the plus sign +). Memory trick: 'Perpendicular' has a 'p' for 'pointy corner'.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: C. Parallel lines meet eventually if extended far enough
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 By definition, parallel lines NEVER meet, no matter how far you extend them. They stay the same distance apart forever — like the two rails of a train track. If lines eventually meet, they are NOT parallel (they could be intersecting or converging lines).

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

choices.label: D. Perpendicular lines can meet at any angle, not just 90°
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Perpendicular lines meet at EXACTLY 90° (a right angle) — no other angle! Lines that cross at other angles are simply 'intersecting lines.' Only when the angle is precisely 90° do we call them perpendicular. The symbol ⊥ shows this right angle.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

challenge.question: What is the perimeter of a square with side 9 cm?

rounds.situation: The community hall wants a stunning tessellated floor — a pattern where shapes fit together perfectly with NO gaps and NO overlaps, like a jigsaw puzzle. You need to figure out which shapes can tessellate. Can squares tile a floor? Triangles? Hexagons? Regular pentagons? The answer might surprise you!
rounds.goal: Understand tessellations — which regular shapes can tile a plane with no gaps or overlaps.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: A tessellation is a pattern of shapes that covers a surface with no gaps and no overlaps. Regular shapes that tessellate: squares (4 × 90° = 360°), equilateral triangles (6 × 60° = 360°), and regular hexagons (3 × 120° = 360°). The angles meeting at each point must add up to exactly 360°!
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why can squares, equilateral triangles, and regular hexagons tessellate but regular pentagons cannot? Hint: think about angles meeting at a point.
rounds.image_prompt: Cartoon floor being tiled with beautiful tessellation patterns — section of squares, section of triangles, section of hexagons, failed pentagon section with gaps, young architect examining patterns with magnifying glass, colorful, Pixar-style

choices.label: A. Isosceles triangle — it has exactly 2 equal sides (7cm, 7cm, 10cm)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Triangles by sides: Equilateral = ALL 3 sides equal. Isosceles = exactly 2 sides equal. Scalene = NO sides equal. This triangle (7cm, 7cm, 10cm) has 2 equal sides, so it's isosceles. Fun fact: an isosceles triangle also has 2 equal angles (the base angles)!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Equilateral triangle — because 7+7 > 10 so all sides matter equally
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Equilateral means ALL THREE sides are equal (e.g., 7cm, 7cm, 7cm). This triangle has sides 7, 7, and 10 — the third side is different. So it's ISOSCELES (2 equal sides), not equilateral. The rule 7+7 > 10 is the Triangle Inequality (it checks if a triangle can exist), which is a different concept.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: C. Scalene triangle — because 10 is different from the other sides
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Scalene means ALL THREE sides are different (e.g., 5cm, 7cm, 10cm). This triangle has TWO sides the same (7cm and 7cm), making it ISOSCELES. In a scalene triangle, no two sides would be equal.

skill_explanation.resilience: Facing challenges head-on strengthens your resilience over time.

choices.label: D. Right triangle — because 7² + 7² might equal 10²
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 'Right triangle' classifies by ANGLES, not sides. Let's check: 7² + 7² = 49 + 49 = 98, but 10² = 100. Since 98 ≠ 100, it's NOT a right triangle either. By sides, it's ISOSCELES (2 equal sides: 7cm, 7cm). Triangles can be classified by sides OR by angles — these are separate systems.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

rounds.situation: It is the day of the Grand Design Showcase! The entire city is invited to see your studio's best work. You must present your complete portfolio — from shape catalogues to tessellated floors, from coordinate city maps to triangular gardens. The mayor, school principals, Client Priya, and even a TV crew are here! This is your moment to show everything you have learned about geometry!
rounds.goal: Apply all geometry concepts in one final creative presentation that wows the audience!
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: True mastery means connecting all concepts together — shapes, angles, area, perimeter, symmetry, coordinates, and tessellations. When you see how they all relate, geometry becomes a powerful tool for understanding and shaping the world around you.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back at all 14 projects, which geometry concept surprised you the most? Which one will you use most in everyday life?

choices.label: A. The missing angle = 180° − 65° − 45° = 70° (angles in a triangle add up to 180°)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The three angles in ANY triangle always add up to exactly 180°. If two angles are 65° and 45°, the third = 180° − 65° − 45° = 180° − 110° = 70°. Check: 65° + 45° + 70° = 180° ✓. This works for ALL triangles — equilateral, isosceles, scalene, right, obtuse, or acute!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.creativity: Thinking outside the box leads to more original solutions.

choices.label: B. The missing angle = 360° − 65° − 45° = 250° (angles add to 360°)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 360° is the angle sum for a QUADRILATERAL (4 sides), not a triangle. Triangle angles add to 180°. So: 180° − 65° − 45° = 70°. Also, 250° would be a reflex angle, which is impossible as a single angle inside a triangle!

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

choices.label: C. The missing angle = 65° + 45° = 110° (add the two known angles)
choices.learning_concept: Finding Missing Angles — Subtract From Total
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Adding the known angles (65° + 45° = 110°) gives the total of those two, but the missing angle = 180° MINUS that sum. Missing angle = 180° − 110° = 70°. Check: 65° + 45° + 70° = 180° ✓. Always subtract from 180° to find the missing angle.

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: D. The missing angle = (65° + 45°) ÷ 2 = 55° (average of the other two)
choices.feedback: Not quite! 💡 Finding the average is not how we find missing angles. The rule is: all three angles must ADD UP to 180°. So: missing angle = 180° − 65° − 45° = 70°. If it were 55°, the total would be 65+45+55 = 165°, which is too little.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

glossary_terms.definition: A flat shape that has length and width but no depth. Examples include triangles, rectangles, circles, and hexagons. '2D' stands for two-dimensional.
The total distance around the outside of a shape. To find the perimeter, add up the lengths of all the sides. For a rectangle: perimeter = 2 × (length + width).
The amount of space inside a flat shape, measured in square units (like sq m or sq cm). For a rectangle: area = length × width. For a triangle: area = 1/2 × base × height.
The amount of turn between two lines that meet at a point. Measured in degrees (°). A right angle is 90°, a straight angle is 180°, and a full turn is 360°.
An imaginary line that divides a shape into two identical halves that are mirror images of each other. A square has 4 lines of symmetry. A circle has infinitely many.
An ordered pair of numbers (x, y) that describes the exact position of a point on a grid. The x-value tells how far across (horizontal) and the y-value tells how far up (vertical).
A pattern of shapes that fit together perfectly with no gaps and no overlaps, covering a surface completely. Squares, equilateral triangles, and regular hexagons can all tessellate.
Any shape with exactly 4 sides and 4 angles. Squares, rectangles, parallelograms, trapezoids, and rhombuses are all types of quadrilaterals.
A triangle where all three sides are the same length and all three angles are equal (60° each). It has 3 lines of symmetry and is the most balanced triangle type.

endings.title: Star Architect
endings.message: You are the undisputed Star Architect of the city! Your geometry skills are extraordinary — every angle is precise, every area is calculated perfectly, and every design is both beautiful and mathematically sound. The mayor presents you with the 'Young Architect of the Year' award, the TV crew features your studio, and schools invite you to teach geometry workshops. You proved that shapes, angles, and measurements are not just numbers — they are the language of design!

endings.title: Popular Studio
endings.message: Your Geometry Design Studio is the most popular firm in the neighbourhood! Clients line up because they know your designs are accurate and creative. Your reputation is solid, your team works well together, and your portfolio is growing. You might not be a geometry genius yet, but you are well on your way to becoming one!

endings.title: Average Practice
endings.message: Your design studio is doing okay — not great, not terrible. Some designs are precise, others have small measurement errors. Clients are satisfied but not amazed. Your geometry skills improved through the 14 projects, but there is still room to grow. The foundation is solid — with more practice, you could become a star architect. Every expert was once a beginner!

endings.title: Struggling Studio
endings.message: Your design studio is struggling. Too many measurement errors crept into your designs — wrong areas, incorrect angles, lopsided symmetry. Clients were not happy and some projects had to be redone. The good news? Every mistake taught you something. Geometry is a skill that improves with practice. Do not give up — come back and try again!

endings.title: Studio Closed
endings.message: The design studio had to close its doors. Wrong measurements led to wrong designs, wrong designs led to unhappy clients, and unhappy clients stopped coming. But here is the truth — every great architect failed many times before succeeding. Geometry is about precision, and precision comes from practice. Come back, sharpen your skills, and try again. Your next attempt will be better!
